title: Can You Overdose on Decodables (Yes)
author: Kata Solow
summary: Guest writer Kata Solow, Executive Director of the Goyen Foundation, examines the growing practice of keeping K-3 students in decodable texts far longer than necessary, sparked by a 3rd grade teacher whose colleagues insisted students read ONLY decodables. Solow argues that overteaching phonics in this way denies students access to real books and leaves them unprepared for standardized tests full of non-decodable passages, while acknowledging teachers face genuinely confusing, under-researched guidance on when to transition students to uncontrolled text.
points: A 3rd grade teacher's colleagues wanted students reading ONLY decodable texts because they hadn't been explicitly taught every phonics pattern in a given passage.
Argues that keeping students exclusively in decodables denies them complex vocabulary, syntax, and real books -- and leaves them unprepared for state tests full of dense, non-decodable text.
Notes there is limited research on precisely when students should transition to uncontrolled text, and that state policy (e.g., Colorado's curriculum standards) can codify overteaching of phonics.
Concludes that research alone won't resolve the question fast enough, so teachers should share practical strategies with each other for bridging decodables to trade books.
quotes: Her colleagues in 3rd grade wanted their students to ONLY read decodable texts.
She wanted them to encounter complex vocabulary and syntax and experience the rich characters and the exciting plotting themselves.
there’s limited research on how to use decodable texts effectively.
So understandably, they err on the side of caution and keep students in decodables for longer than necessary.
Teachers can share how they’re using a combination of decodable and uncontrolled texts.
research alone is NOT going to save us here. For one thing, we can’t wait around for researchers to answer these questions for us.
